newsitem.title: UK: Med sour crude bouyant on tight supply, tenders.
newsitem.headline: Med sour crude bouyant on tight supply, tenders.

text.p: Sour crude markets in southern Europe were bouyant on Tuesday, supported by the continuing absence of Iraqi Kirkuk, tight prompt supply of Russian Urals and two buying tenders, traders said.
Benchmark Russian Urals was valued at Dated Brent -60/-55 cents a barrel basis cif Augusta, the smallest midsummer discount for several years, and there was little sign of weakness in the short-term.
"Urals is tight and I don't see Iraqi barrels in the short term," said a trader.
"Margins have stabilised, even maybe improved a little and refiners are still there to buy," he added.

Despite signs of progress towards U.N. approval of Baghdad's revised food distribution plan, which would remove one of the last major obstacles to a resumption of exports suspended since late May, traders doubt Iraqi crude will be available before the second half of August.

"Iraq is the only real alternative to Urals but even if they (U.N.) approve the aid plan this week and Baghdad says the first cargoes are available tomorrow it will still take five or six days to fix a vessel," said a trader.

Pricing formulas have also to be agreed. Market talk suggested Iraq's State Oil Marketing Organisation (SOMO) would most likely propose an unchanged relationship to the value of Saudi Arab Light which would peg Kirkuk at a competitive Dated Brent -$2.00 a barrel fob Ceyhan.
"That would appear generous but the (Dated) -55 cents for Urals isn't going to hold a moment once they start selling again," said a trader.

Time lost since June 8, when the second round of the oil-for-food deal formally began, means SOMO will probably have to sell around 1.5 million barrels per day (bpd) to raise the $1 billion allowed during the first 90 day period.

But until that wave of crude appears, refiners will be left scrabbling around for prompt barrels. Traders said two Urals purchase tenders were due to close on Tuesday, one into Morocco and the other into Greece.
Nigerian crudes were also holding recent firm levels with Bonny Light pegged at Dated Brent +47/+50 cents a barrel.
Traders said about a dozen late August cargoes of Nigerian crude were still unsold but most were being offered on a delivered basis into the U.S. Gulf.
"The Far East is pretty much done for the month and Europe may take one or two more," said a trader.
"But most of the cargoes are being offered into the U.S. where there's a fair amount of interest thanks to the pick up in gasoline demand," he added.
Distillate-rich Forcados was also holding its ground just above Dated Brent +30 cents with only one 600,000 barrel third decad stem seen available.
